content.thinking:
I'm sketching proportions for a red panda standing on a rounded, mossy stone, legs spread for balance with the tail trailing behind for stability.

Thinking about little decorative extras too — scattered pebbles, moss tufts, a fallen leaf, maybe tiny mushrooms, and a Genshin-style gold filigree collar with a tasseled dendro gem charm for a bit of elemental flair.

For the pose, I'll keep all four paws planted on the stone with a relaxed stance, tail curling up in an S-shape for balance, and the head tilted slightly for character. For the stone itself, I'm leaning toward building it as a flattened, elongated boulder shape rather than a simple sphere, sizing it so the panda's feet sit near the top while keeping the whole base shallow enough to respect the floor-sinking limit.

Rather than trying to scale a sphere non-uniformly, I'll use a lathe profile with a flat bottom and rounded bulging top, then jitter the vertices with noise and apply flat shading to give it that irregular, natural rock texture.

For painting, I'll make the top faces moss green with mottling while the sides stay grey-blue stone, using cel shading based on facet normals. I want to keep the top plateau relatively flat and unjittered so the feet have stable, non-floating footing, limiting the noise jitter to just the sides of the stone.

Rather than a simple lathe, I'm planning an irregular rock shape: generate a LatheGeometry with 14 azimuthal segments and multiple rows, then apply elliptical scaling and noise jitter to the vertex positions (skipping the top row) to make it look natural, keeping the built-in UVs for painting.

Now I'm thinking through red panda anatomy in a cute stylized Genshin-like design: rusty-red head and back, white cheeks and muzzle with dark tear markings, white brow spots, black belly and legs, a bushy ringed tail, and black paws with small claws.

For color palette I'm going with rust-orange, deep chestnut for legs and belly, cream for highlights, and a dark nose. I'm working out chibi-style proportions with an oversized head, setting the body length and establishing the skeleton coordinates starting from the hips relative to the stone surface height.

Now I'm refining the leg length and body height based on real red panda proportions, figuring out where the back, belly, and shoulder heights should sit relative to the stone. I'm setting up the spine as a curved chain of points running from hips to chest with a slight arch, and starting the neck segment next.

Then I'm planning the skeleton structure: making "hips" the root joint and attaching the spine chain to it with the chain's first point matching the hips position, following the pattern from the docs where a chain's initial joint coincides with its parent.

For the tail, I'm sketching a chain off hips with a curved S-shaped path extending back and gently upward, keeping it clear of the floor while giving it a bushy radius around 0.05.

Writing ring pattern logic...

Also planning the tail tip to be dark chestnut for the last 12%, then moving to the four legs with hip and knee joint chains.

I'm now placing the leg joints: shoulders, elbows, wrists down to ground-contact paws, with paw radius and slight sink into the ground. I'm working out the two-segment IK geometry for the front legs, computing joint distances to find the limb lengths needed to reach the paw targets.

For the hind legs, I'm considering whether to use a simple two-segment chain or a more anatomically correct three-segment thigh-shin-foot setup with bend hints for the knee pointing forward and elbow pointing back, but deciding to keep it simpler with two segments plus a paw tip for the plantigrade foot.

For the legs' visual thickness, I'm planning to sweep varying radii along each chain to give chunkier, tapered limbs with dark chestnut coloring and fur tufts, and for the body I want to sweep along the spine chain with radii that bulge wider at the hips and chest for a chubby silhouette.

With round caps extending beyond the spine's endpoints, I'm checking that the total body length comes out around 0.5-0.6, which fits a stylized red panda. For coloring, I'm considering countershading the back rust red against a darker chestnut belly, layering fur-edge texturing inside a cel-shading paint function to get painterly fur transitions along the body's normal axis.

For richer color variation, I'm layering two nested fur-edge gradients to get a three-tone coat: deeper rust along the back, lighter amber on the flanks, and chestnut underneath, zigzagging along the z-axis for texture. Now I'm moving to the head, building the skull as a scaled sphere with fluffy cheek tufts and a short muzzle, planning to paint cheek and muzzle markings based on position relative to the head center.

Working out the facial coloring: cream patches for cheeks and muzzle against a red cap on the crown, with dark tear-line markings running from eyes to mouth, using zigzagged position-based boundaries so the fur edges look natural rather than sharp.

For the eyes I'm leaning toward anime-style decals placed on the skull, picking a vivid jade-green iris (tying into a dendro theme) instead of a realistic dark brown, paired with subtle blush and mirrored placement for symmetry.

Now I'm working out the muzzle structure—a cream snout with a small dark nose, an ink-line mouth sweep, and separate upper/lower jaw pieces hinged at a jaw joint. For the ears, I'm planning big rounded-triangle shapes with rust outer color, cream edges, and white inner tufts, built as extruded/beveled outlines tilted outward at the top of the head.

Working out ear orientation vectors...

Now thinking about facial details: adding small cream eyebrow spots as flattened spheres above each eye, dark tear-mark sweeps draping from inner-lower eye corner to mouth, and a ring of small outward-pointing cream spike-cones along the lower cheek for that fluffy tuft look.

I'm also planning dark fur tufts at the chest, elbows and legs, plus a few thin white whisker sweeps near the muzzle. For the paws I'll use small spheres for toes with tiny cream claw-cones, skipping underside pads since they're hidden, and finishing with a Genshin-style gold collar charm looping around the neck with a small round bell.

Then I'm adding a jade dendro pendant with gold filigree framing and two tasseled rings hanging from a teal-green ribbon collar, plus a tiny glowing leaf sprout nestled between the ears for a cute elemental touch. I'll scatter a handful of floating glowing motes shaped like four-point stars or leaves above the head to suggest dendro magic, and add moss-cap grass tufts as extra ground detail.

I'm working out the base now: small pebbles, miniature mushrooms, clover sprigs, and a faintly glowing rune-etched arc on the stone to nod to the ruins aesthetic, keeping the animal as the hero while making the mossy stone base feel like a rich diorama. I'm also sizing the stone's top ellipse wide enough to comfortably support the panda's paw stance.

For proportions, I'm sketching out total height from stone base through tail and ears, making sure sparkles stay below a certain height so the piece reads around 0.8m tall without feeling overblown. Then I'm roughing out the skeleton -- hips, spine segments, neck, head, jaw, ears, a long tail chain, and four legs with hip-knee-paw joints -- debating whether to add separate toe joints per the digit-separation guidance.

Deciding to skip whisker and eyelid joints and keep digits as static paw geometry rather than animated joints, then settling the neutral rest stance with legs spread and tail curved in an S shape.

Setting up imports and utilities for the build -- bringing in the builder, frame, IK limb solver, math helpers, path curves, paint/shading tools, toon shading kit, glow effects, and geometry merging utilities, then starting to define the bright Genshin-style color palette.

Writing palette definitions...

Defining the boulder geometry function with a lathe profile to create rounded stone shapes with a flattened top plateau.

Rather than deriving an analytic top function, I'll just jitter the radial noise on the rock rows while keeping the top cap rows fixed and unjittered. With 14 segments and 9 profile rows, that's around 250 triangles, which is plenty manageable.

For the lathe orientation, I'm relying on the standard convention of ordering points from bottom to top so normals face outward, matching how Three.js examples build these shapes; the bottom face winding doesn't matter since it won't be visible. For jittering each vertex, I'm applying a small radial scale perturbation plus a slight y offset using a hash based on ring and segment index, accounting for how LatheGeometry duplicates seam vertices.

For the seam issue, I'm switching to jittering based on actual vertex position rather than index so duplicated seam vertices get identical noise values and match up seamlessly. I'm deciding to attach the stone geometry to a new root joint (placed below hips) rather than binding it directly to hips, so it stays rigid and unaffected by hip animation, then I'm starting to write a custom paint function for the stone that blends in moss coloring based on the surface normal's upward component combined with positional noise.

Now I'm refining that moss blend using a threshold on normal.y plus ragged noise to decide where moss appears versus bare stone, wrapping the whole thing in a cel-shaded paint so lit and shadow colors resolve correctly per-material, and adding cell-based crack lines along cell borders to give the stone a weathered, fractured look.

I want to add dimensional moss "pillows" as flattened overlapping spheres on top rather than just a flat paint layer, plus drips, and tuft cards for grass blades and tiny clovers -- double-sided SVG blade shapes in layered greens with dark outlines. I'm deciding where to place fur/tuft spikes: cheek ruff, leg tufts, chest, ear tufts, and tail tip, skipping tail fluff cards to keep things cleaner, and now moving into defining the actual geometry in code.

Building the skeleton chain...

I should use the model's local coordinate convention where "left" refers to the model's own left side, computing the head center as roughly [0, ST+0.28, 0.38] using the local forward/up offsets, then start listing the head's component parts like the skull, all parented to the head bone.

For the skull, I'm scaling a sphere to give the broad red panda face shape, with the face paint evaluated in model space. I'm also sketching out the cheek ruff spikes, the cream snout positioned slightly below and forward of the head center, a small dark nose at the tip with a tiny glossy highlight, and now I'm working out the lower jaw joint position and chin sphere scale.

Now I'm figuring out the mouth line as an inked sweep under the snout, then placing the eyes as decals on the skull surface using azimuth and elevation angles so they sit toward the front sides without intruding too far into the cheeks. For face coloring I'm deriving positions relative to the head center to decide where cream, rust, and white patches go, plus adding eyebrow spots and tear-line markings running from the inner-bottom of each eye.

I'm defining the tear-stripe region as a front-facing band with a darker reddish-brown color, computed from a conditional on depth and position, then setting up the paint function to return color strings that get resolved through lighting and shadow. Finally I'm starting on the ear geometry, parenting ear joints to the head and outlining a rounded triangular ear shape.

Working out ear orientation...

I realize that keeping x fixed while skewing y breaks orthogonality, which would shear rather than rotate the ears. A cleaner fix is proper rotation about the z-axis, defining x and y as cosine/sine pairs for the rotation angle, with sign flipped depending on left versus right ear.

Working out the orthogonality and cross-product sign checks for both sides, then adding a slight forward pitch by introducing a small rotation about the x-axis.

Still working out ear rotation signs...

For the inner ear, I'll add a smaller cream-colored shell offset slightly outward in depth to suggest the fluffy fringe typical of red pandas, keeping it simple rather than adding individual fringe spikes. I'll also give the eyes a few eyelash flicks extending from the anime-style eye shape.

Moving to legs, I want rust-red haunch spheres on the hind thighs and dark chestnut fur coloring down the legs, since red panda limbs are typically blackish-brown with darker paws. I'll define leg sweep geometry using a chain of tapering radii for a natural tapered limb shape.

For paws, I'm sculpting a flattened sphere shape for the pad with toes as small spheres clustered near the front and tiny cream cone claws, trying to keep part count manageable by merging same-colored toes per paw.

For the tail, I'm building a bushy sweep along a chain with varying radii and considering adding small fur tuft spikes at intervals along the edge for texture.

I'm plotting a smooth catmull-rom curve for the tail path, adjusting the height so it doesn't end up too tall, aiming for a cute S-curve shape with a slight lateral offset near the tip for natural asymmetry.

Now I'm setting up five tail joints with radii that bulge in the middle and narrow toward base and tip, giving it that bushy red panda look, then planning alternating amber and rust-colored rings for the paint pattern across the tail.

For the body I'll keep the underside a darker chestnut tone and skip extra dorsal striping to keep things simple, then add thin cream-colored whisker strokes sweeping from the muzzle sides.

Now for the collar, I'm thinking through how to wrap a ring around the neck geometry separately from the body sweep, since the neck has its own joint sequence distinct from the spine. Writing sweep geometry...

Actually, let me build the band from three rings instead: a green ribbon base ring at the neck midpoint, flanked by two thinner gold rings slightly offset forward and back, each at roughly the same radius, before moving on to the pendant.

Now I'm figuring out where to hang the pendant — a gold trefoil frame with a glowing green gem — at the lowest front point of the ring. I need to locate that point by finding the ring's bottom-front position relative to the neck's forward tilt, since the pendant should hang down at the chest and might otherwise get hidden under the chin.

Checking the chest sphere cap height confirms the ray at that y hits the chest front near z=0.27, slightly below its center, so it lands correctly on the torso rather than the collar ring near the neck.

Let me reposition the collar lower, around the neck-chest junction where the body surface actually exists -- placing it at the neck chain point with a ring radius around 0.08, with the pendant hanging off the front via a ray hit at the chest. I'll add two tassels hanging from the pendant's bottom and iterate with a preview to check placement.

For the tassels, I'm thinking small gold beads with cone shapes tilted slightly against the curved chest surface, hung from a gold ring below the pendant. I also want to add a glowing gold-green filigree seal decal lying flat on the stone top, partially hidden under the moss, with the panda standing on it for a nice mystical touch.

I'm also planning floating motes—five small glowing star shapes in green and yellow scattered above the tail and head area, plus a tiny sprout with two leaves growing from a crack at the front-left of the stone.

Now I'm adding mushrooms near the moss edge, pebbles and small boulders around the base, and grass tufts, aiming for several hundred parts total using scatter functions across the stone's surface. Writing SVG tuft shape...

Now I'm sketching individual blade paths with a darker green outline for depth, and planning the eye decal and mouth paint strokes to finish off the creature's face details.

Simpler to drape the rough philtrum path onto the snout surface directly rather than compute exact points. Now I'm defining concrete head joint coordinates to anchor the snout center for this calculation.

I'm now working out the body proportions and leg placement — checking shoulder height, belly clearance above the ground, and positioning hip and shoulder joints so the legs read as short but visible without clipping into the body.

For the legs, I'm computing hind and front limb segment lengths and bend directions so the knees and elbows flex naturally, with hind paws planted plantigrade-style under the hips and front paws bending the elbow backward for a believable stance.

I'll need unique joint names per limb—shoulderL/elbowL/handL for front, hipL/kneeL/footL for hind—treating both as "leg" roles, with front limbs thinner and hind thighs thicker with a haunch bulge for the sweep geometry.

Keeping colors under the flat-color limit by relying on paint/cel shading for most hues, I'm sketching a helper function for building spheres with scaled dimensions and low-poly segment counts for the small joint balls.

Now I'm working out eye placement from the skull part using local coordinates scaled to the skull's half-width, and figuring out ear joint positions relative to the head frame, accounting for left/right mirroring with the sign variable.

I'm placing the ear extrusion at the computed joint, then adding small cream eyebrow spheres embedded above the eyes using the same hit-point and elevation/azimuth approach.

For teeth and tongue, I'm skipping them since the mouth stays closed in the neutral pose, and I'll leave skull rim details out too. Next I'll move on to drafting the tail ring code and run a build/typecheck/preview pass.

Now I'm setting up the color palette (rust, amber, chestnut, cream, dark plum) and writing the face paint function, defining cream regions for cheeks and muzzle using zigzag patterns based on local position offsets from the head center.

I'm also adding dark tear-line markings running down from the eyes toward the muzzle, computed with a parametric path that curves outward and tapers in thickness as it descends, mirrored across both sides of the face.

For the fur coloring, I'm layering cel-shaded colors using nested fur-edge functions—starting with amber for the chest, blending into rust tones for the flanks and coat, with thresholds and teeth parameters controlling where each color band transitions based on surface normal direction.

For the legs, I'm painting a gradient from the base leg color down to a darker paw tone, blending vertically based on model position, and considering whether to keep it soft or snap it into a harder cel-shaded step for crispness. I'm also noting that shared painted regions on the atlas should help keep things cheaper to render, and starting to think about adding mossy bump details along stone overhangs.

Now I'm placing mushrooms and pebbles near the stone base, positioning a couple mushrooms with cream-spotted caps on the floor near the front-left of the stone, scattering pebbles nearby, and considering where small plants might sprout from the stone's side without overlapping awkwardly. I'm also sketching out a sigil design with radial gold and green circle strokes and leaf motifs.

Writing SVG rings and leaves...

Still refining stone dimensions...

The top row stays unjittered while the 0.95 row gets mild noise, and I'll keep the moss pillows overlapping only at the rim (r>0.6) so the center stays flat, placing the sigil just above the top surface at y=ST+0.003 with moss coloring on top.

Setting the stone height at exactly 0.22, with the panda feet sinking 0.003 below that surface. I'll write a helper to compose transform matrices for geometry (position, rotation, scale) and start building the cone geometries next.

For the claw cones pointing forward, I'm rotating them 90° about the X axis so they point along +z instead of +y. Then I'm positioning the toe spheres across each paw, spacing them with small x-offsets and placing them slightly forward and above the paw surface.

Still writing paw geometry...

For tail fluff, I'm scattering spikes along the tail's sweep curve, placing them on the dorsal ridge to create a jagged zigzag silhouette, each colored flat rust.

Since each spike has its own source path, I need to use flat or position-based coloring rather than sweep-relative paint to avoid mismatched evaluation—so I'll use a fixed cel color for them. Time to start coding this, including randomized scatter and the neck sweep chain.

For the body, I'm tuning radius values along the spine to get a rounded elliptical taper from rump to shoulders, using default circle cross-sections which should shade smoothly for the cel look. I'm skipping the chest cream detail and moving to write the sweep code, making sure the head collision check handles a null hit result properly.

Now I'm working out the mouth geometry: placing the snout center, nose sphere, and philtrum curve as points draped onto the muzzle surface, then positioning the chin below to separate the upper and lower jaw at the mouth line.

I'm defining the jaw joint parented to the head with its pivot and aim points, adjusting the head's forward/up orientation, and setting up the neck sweep endpoint to align with the head joint. I'm also planning a collar ring positioned partway along the neck using a ring-generation helper.

Now I'm designing a gem pendant for the chest: a gold quatrefoil frame with beveled extrusion holding a small glowing green diamond gem, and I'm working out the axis orientation so the pendant faces forward correctly.

Still writing pendant shape...

I need to figure out where to anchor the pendant - it should hang below the collar near the neck front, not sitting on the chest, so I'll position it just under the chin area and verify placement in preview.

For the tassels, I'm planning thin downward spikes in teal and gold from the pendant's bottom, and considering card-based tassels with bead and strand textures, oriented to hang down and rigidly attached to the neck bone.

I'm adding glow to the gem, sparkles, and sigil, then designing small four-pointed star shapes with sharp tips for sparkles, flat-colored in pale green with glow, scattered at varied tilted positions around the upper torso while keeping everything under the height limit, plus considering floating leaf accents.

Now I'm figuring out how these decorative parts attach—deciding to bone them all to the root joint for simplicity—then moving on to the ear coloring: a rust cel-shaded outer surface with a cream fringe, keeping the painting logic simple rather than overcomplicating with gradient thresholds, and planning to extrude the inner ear geometry at a thinner offset.

I'll compute the inner ear's attachment point relative to the ear's local coordinate frame so it sits correctly on the front face, then double-check the extrude options use the ear joint as its bone. With that settled, I'm ready to write the full implementation, run a type check, and iterate visually from there.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/redPandaSonnet/ && sed -n 1,80p src/ik.ts | head -100; sed -n 60,140p src/frame.ts; ls ~/tmp/public/nilo/agentic-3js-builder 2>/dev/null | head
